newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada urged to make grain shipments reliable.
newsitem.headline: Canada urged to make grain shipments reliable.

text.p: The Canadian government must take steps to ensure reliable rail and port shipments of grain if its agriculture sector is to compete on world markets, the head of one of Canada's largest grain handlers said.

"We'll have to get some of these long term institutional, regulatory, legislated issues updated to the 1990s or the year 2000 and get on with the business of agriculture," Pioneer Grain Co president Curt Vossen told Reuters in an interview.
Canada's reputation as a supplier of grain to the world was hurt in recent years by strikes and ship delays, he said.
"I think a lot of customers of ours are perplexed by our labor, transportation and supply problems in Canada," he said.
Amendments to Canada's labor code requiring striking longshoremen and stevedores to transfer grain to ships were not enacted into law in April before an election was called.
The last such strike in Vancouver in 1995 caused a six week backlog in Canada's grainhandling pipeline.

Railway delays between January and April 1997 attributed to severe weather and equipment failure saw 48 ships sit empty at Pacific ports, some for more than 50 days, and cost the Canadian Wheat Board C$23 million in demurrage, the CWB said.
Canada's Transport, Agriculture and CWB ministers met with grain and rail industry leaders July 25 to study the problem.

A grain industry group two years ago suggested a system of rewards and penalties to encourage efficiency among railways, grain firms and farmers as well as selling the federal government's fleet of 1,000 hopper cars to the rail companies.

Although those recommendations were not acted on, many industry leaders said they invited the federal government to do so now. Meanwhile, the federal government plans to review its cap on freight rail rates for grain later this fall rather than in 1999.
Pioneer's Vossen said port and rail regulatory changes were likely to have similar repercussions on the industry as did the elimination of Canada's 98-year-old grain rail freight subsidy in 1995.
The end of the subsidy led to regional shifts in crop production and a variety of capital investments estimated at about C$2 billion.

"If you see all these test plots on the Prairies by seed, ag chem and fertilizer companies testing products, new facilities being built like flour mills and crush plants, it's a very optimistic time for Canadian agriculture," Vossen said.
"The industry's much more likely to see change and improvements than 10 years ago. It's a good time for Canadian agriculture...it'll continue to improve," he added.
